mcqs.question: A company has Java, Python, and Go services each implementing their own retry and TLS logic via separate libraries, and the policies have drifted apart. What does a service mesh fix here?
options: It applies retry, TLS, and traffic policy consistently at the network layer, regardless of the service's language
It rewrites all three services into a single language to eliminate drift
It removes the need for retries entirely by making all network calls succeed on the first attempt
It merges all three services into one shared codebase
mcqs.explanation: A mesh intercepts traffic at the network layer via sidecars, so the same retry/TLS/traffic policy applies uniformly no matter what language a service is written in — no more per-library drift. It doesn't rewrite services into one language, doesn't make network calls infallible, and doesn't merge codebases.

mcqs.question: In a service mesh, what is the relationship between the data plane and the control plane?
options: The control plane intercepts application traffic directly; the data plane only stores logs
The data plane (sidecar proxies) does the actual traffic interception and forwarding; the control plane configures all the sidecars' routing, certificates, and policy
They are two names for the same component with no functional difference
The data plane runs once per cluster; the control plane runs once per service instance
mcqs.explanation: Sidecars (data plane) are the per-instance proxies that actually intercept and forward traffic; the control plane is the central brain that pushes configuration — routing rules, certs, policy — out to every sidecar. The control plane doesn't intercept traffic itself, the two aren't interchangeable, and it's the sidecar (not the control plane) that's per-instance while the control plane is typically cluster-wide.

mcqs.question: A platform team wants to send 5% of production traffic to a new service version and watch its error rate before a full rollout. Which mesh capability is this?
mcqs.explanation: Sending a small percentage of live traffic to a new version to observe it before a full cutover is exactly canary routing, a traffic-management feature. mTLS handles identity/encryption, circuit breaking stops sending traffic to a failing instance, and service discovery is about finding live instances, not splitting traffic between versions.

mcqs.question: A single team running five services adopts a full service mesh (control plane plus sidecars everywhere) because it's considered a microservices best practice. What is the likely outcome?
options: The team gets significant benefit immediately, since mesh adoption has no downside at any scale
The mesh automatically reduces the team's number of services
The mesh eliminates the need for service discovery entirely with no configuration
The team takes on real operational overhead (a control plane to run, sidecars adding latency, new failure modes) to solve a policy-drift problem they don't actually have yet
mcqs.explanation: A mesh's main value — consistent policy across many teams and languages — doesn't materialize for one team with five services, while the operational cost (control plane, sidecar latency, new failure surface) is paid regardless of scale. There's no benefit that appears with zero downside, a mesh doesn't reduce service count, and it still requires configuration even if it can incorporate service discovery.
